speechtext: Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Superintendent Gen eral of Indian Affairs) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 4, to amend the Indian Act.
Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The amendments suggested to the Indian Act are all of a minor character, as I recall them now; it is some little time since I have seen them. They relate to the disposal of the property of an Indian on a reserve to someone off the reserve; to the manner in which the council meetings of the Indians may be held and the giving of a casting vote to the presiding officer; and there are also some regulations to control what is termed a potlatch that still exists on one reserve on Vancouver island. As I have said the amendments are more or less minor in character and a fuller explanation will be given when the second reading is moved.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. BENNETT DISMISSAL OF CERTAIN HOUSE OF COMMONS EMPLOYEES

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. BENNETT DISMISSAL OF CERTAIN HOUSE OF COMMONS EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the
orders of the day are called, I beg to rise to a question of privilege. I am informed that this morning at ten o'clock, and thereafter, a number of employees of the House of Commons were called into the office of the sergeant-at-arms and summarily dismissed, without cause being alleged or given. In some cases this means a very great hardship. I wrote to the leader of the government (Mr. Mackenzie King) this morning as follows:
I regret to have to inform you that I propose raising the question of the privileges of the House of Commons in connection with the dismissal this morning, under instructions from the Speaker, of a number of men who have been employed in the house for some years past.
Some of those persons thus dismissed have been employed for many years, some for six years or thereabouts and others for lesser periods of time. I am not discussing their fitness for their positions, because, as I shall point out presently, if they have been guilty of misconduct or if there is any charge against them, that charge must be investigated. If

Dismissals-Mr. Bennett
it is found warranted by the facts, then, of course, the statute provides that the Speaker may dismiss them.
The words with which I opened my observations are words which I have read in an address made by the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier in this house on Tuesday, February 28, 1888.
I mention that because later he presented a motion to the house, to which I referred the other day. A debate ensued and definite action was taken by the house, holding that the translators came within the ordinary rule and were not exempt from the provisions of the statute. This is the privilege of this house that I want to bring to the attention of this chamber: Our statute provides that the Speaker of this house shall exercise certain powers only under certain conditions. Section 21 of chapter 145 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927, which in terms is the same as the statute referred to by the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier in 1888, reads as follows:
If any complaint or representation is at any time made to the Speaker for the time being of the misconduct or unfitness of any clerk, officer, messenger or other person attendant on the House of Commons, the Speaker may cause an inquiry to be made into the conduct or fitness of such person.
2. If thereupon it appears to the Speaker that such person has been guilty of misconduct, or is unfit to hold' his situation, the Speaker may, if such clerk, officer, messenger or other person has been appointed by the crown, suspend him and report such suspension to the governor general, and, if he has not been appointed by the crown, suspend or remove him.
In other words no man serving this House of Commons is to be dismissed by the Speaker until he has been given notice of the misconduct charged against him and has had an opportunity to give his defence, and then only after action is taken in the manner indicated by the statute. Therefore there has been a clear breach of the privileges of the House of Commons.
There is the statute. This morning, without notice as to the cause, men were called into the office of the sergeant-at-arms and told that their services were ended. The Speaker is bound by the statute; the sergeant-at-arms, carrying out the directions of the Speaker, also is bound by the statute. Some of these men were returned men; one of them has six children and his wife was ill all summer. He is dismissed without notice, just told to go and check out. Obviously, not having had an opportunity to ascertain the fact because I could not ask either the sergeant-at-arms or the Speaker with relation to it, all I can say is that I was told on what I regard as good authority that a large number of these men
have been thus dismissed from their positions, in this cold, winter weather, without warning, except as I understand, that notice was sent by one of the members of this house, the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Cas-grain) some days ago that they were engaged only from day to day. But he was not the Speaker of this house at that time and I think it is quite clear that he had no authority to send any such notice.
In the case to which I referred, in 1888, the matter was discussed at great length. There seemed to be no doubt in the mind of anyone that an employee of this house could not be dismissed unless he had a chance to be heard, unless he had notice what his fault was. In that case Mr., later Sir Adolphe Chapleau, wrote a letter to the Speaker making his complaints against the individuals in question; the Speaker at once passed it on to them and they filed their defence; on the strength of that the matter was then sent by the Speaker to the committee on debates, and subsequently it apparently reached the committee on privileges and was dealt with. This is what Sir Wilfrid Laurier said as to the method that was adopted:
In fact the complaint which was made -against them is not in reference to their services as officers of this house, but the charge is that they went out of their proper sphere of action and grossly insulted some, members of this house. The charge was brought forward by my hon. friend, the Secretary of State, in a letter dated the 22nd May, 1887.
I will not read that because it is not pertinent to what I have to say:
Upon receipt of these complaints, you, sir, very properly referred them to the officers themselves for their answer. They sent you their answers, and you afterwards sent the whole correspondence to the chairman of the debates committee. The debates committee investigated the matter and came to the conclusion that it had better be left in your hands to be dealt with. They reported to the house, but that report never was taken up, it never was even moved in the house. It must be regretted that this report was not considered by the house, because then the whole matter could have been dealt with by the house upon its merits, and the house could have determined at once whether these gentlemen had been guilty of such an offence as warranted their dismissal.
I am not going to do more than point out that in all the discussion that took place there seemed to be no doubt that the provisions of the statute in any event must be observed, that complaint must be made and when the complaint is made opportunity should be given to the person charged to defend himself, and thereafter the action mentioned in the statute may be taken.
Dismissals-Mr. Bennett

Now, sir, I bring to your attention the fact that one of the privileges of this house has thus been violated. It was regarded by the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier and by all those who spoke in the house then as a matter of first rate importance, not as something trifling and insignificant. That men could be dismissed without notice and without cause assigned seemed to be something that every member of the house regarded as impossible because of the statute-it was not then chapter 145, but I have taken the trouble to have it compared, and that statute still governs this house. How are we to deal with it? Obviously the proper course is indicated by the action taken by the House of Commons in 1888. And it must have been before this house since-I have not had time to look it up-because I observe this copy of Hansard is underlined with pen and pencil by some persons who evidently have been giving it careful consideration in years long since past-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. BENNETT DISMISSAL OF CERTAIN HOUSE OF COMMONS EMPLOYEES
speechtext: Perhaps 1930.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. BENNETT DISMISSAL OF CERTAIN HOUSE OF COMMONS EMPLOYEES
speechtext: No, the question what was done in 1930 does not in any sense enter into this.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. BENNETT DISMISSAL OF CERTAIN HOUSE OF COMMONS EMPLOYEES
speechtext: It certainly does.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. BENNETT DISMISSAL OF CERTAIN HOUSE OF COMMONS EMPLOYEES
speechtext: It cannot possibly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. BENNETT DISMISSAL OF CERTAIN HOUSE OF COMMONS EMPLOYEES
speechtext: We shall see.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. BENNETT DISMISSAL OF CERTAIN HOUSE OF COMMONS EMPLOYEES
speechtext: I admit the hon. gentleman is right in saying he can call up his majority-

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. BENNETT DISMISSAL OF CERTAIN HOUSE OF COMMONS EMPLOYEES
speechtext: No one said that.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. BENNETT DISMISSAL OF CERTAIN HOUSE OF COMMONS EMPLOYEES
speechtext: No one has raised the question of this statute in this house since I have been in it. I confess I was not, until I looked into it, aware of the fact that the provisions of the statute were as they are.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. BENNETT DISMISSAL OF CERTAIN HOUSE OF COMMONS EMPLOYEES
speechtext: As the right hon. gentleman says they are.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. BENNETT DISMISSAL OF CERTAIN HOUSE OF COMMONS EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
No, it is not what I say the statute is; I am reading it. In order that there may be no misapprehension I again direct attention to section 21 of chapter 145, which says:
If any complaint or representation is at any time made to the Speaker for the time being of the misconduct or unfitness of any clerk, officer, messenger or other person attendant on the House of Commons, the Speaker may cause an inquiry to be made into the conduct or fitness of such person.
2. If thereupon it appears to the Speaker that such person has been guilty of misconduct, or is unfit to hold his situation, the Speaker may, if such clerk, officer, messenger or other person has been appointed by the crown,

suspend him and report such suspension to the govenor general, and, if he has not been appointed by the crown, suspend or remove him.
That is the relevant section of the act which governs this House of Commons, and any open and, shall I say, deliberate violation of it constitutes a breach of the privileges of the House of Commons.
Now I ask, What is to be done about it? In the case to which I have referred the Speaker said that the papers would be laid upon the table to-morrow. It seems to me that under the circumstances is all we can reasonably hope to have done. The matter then ended. But when Sir Wilfrid had brought the question to the attention of the house and said he proposed to have it discussed, the Speaker said that the papers would be laid upon the table, and I later observe that his language was this: "The papers will be brought down tomorrow." And on March 1:
Mr. Speaker laid before the house certain letters, affidavits and other papers relating to the dismissal of Messrs. A. E. Poirier, E. Tremblay and R. Tremblay, who were up to a recent period employed as French translators of the official debates of the house.
It may be a matter of importance to the house in considering its privileges to realize that these gentlemen were not dismissed in that session of 1887, but in the early part of the session of 1888.
I merely suggest that, having regard to the terms of the statute, it is the duty of the Speaker to lay before this house at the next convenient session, it may be tomorrow or Monday, all the papers with respect to the dismisssal of any employees of this house in accordance with the practice adopted in the construction placed by the house upon the statute that governs our deliberations.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. BENNETT DISMISSAL OF CERTAIN HOUSE OF COMMONS EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as my right
hon. friend has just said he was kind enough to send me a communication at noon to-day mentioning that he intended to bring up in the house this afternoon the question of the dismissal of some employees of the house, which in his opinion constituted a breach of the privileges of the house. In support of his contention that there has been such a breach of the privileges of the house, my right hon. friend has read section 21 of chapter 145 of the House of Commons Act:
If any complaint or representation is at any time made to the Speaker for the time being of the misconduct or unfitness of any clerk, officer, messenger or other person attendant

Dismissals-Mr. Mackenzie King
on the House of Commons, the Speaker may cause an inquiry to be made into the conduct or fitness of such person.
2. If thereupon it appears to the Speaker that such person has been guilty of misconduct, or is unfit to hold his situation, the Speaker may, if such clerk, officer, messenger or other person has been appointed by the crown, suspend him and report such suspension to the governor general, and, if he has not been appointed by the crown, suspend or remove him.
May I draw the attention of my right hon. friend and of the house generally to a distinction which I believe that section was intended to make? It distinguishes between employees who constitute the permanent organization of the House of Commons and its temporary employees. In the organization of this house for the purpose of enabling it to carry on its business there is a distinction to be drawn between the permanent organization that continues year in and year out, and the additional organization that is necessary for carrying on the business of individual sessions. Hon. members will realize that, regardless of periods of vacation and the like, it is essential that there be a permanent staff here, and that, in connection with many matters that affect the House of Commons, there are officers who must be regarded as permanent officials of the House of Commons. With respect to dismissals that have taken place to-day or yesterday, I am informed that there has been no dismissal whatever of any member of the permanent organization of the House of Commons. As I say, there is a second group of clerks, messengers and others, who are appointed for the duration of the session. That group of temporary, as distinguished from permanent employees, includes stenographers, messengers, pages, some charmen that are known as all-year charmen. A clear distinction has always been drawn between the two, one which in the past has governed the actions of the Speaker in dealing with members of the staff of the House of Commons.
My right hon. friend did not read the next section. I do not think he avoided doing so intentionally, but I submit it helps to bring out the meaning of the act. It is as follows:
The Clerk of the House of Commons shall subscribe and take before the Speaker the oath of allegiance, and' all other officers, clerks and messengers of the House of Commons shall subscribe and take before the Clerk of the House of Commons the oath of allegiance.
2. The Clerk of the House of Commons shall keep a register of all such oaths.
I asked the clerk to have in the house this afternoon a record of the registration of oaths of persons included under section 22. The record is at present on the table of the
house. I am advised that not a single one of these persons whose names are there recorded has been dismissed.
I am further advised, and I believe correctly, that in other sessions and other parliaments it has not been customary to have oaths of allegiance of temporary employees, of the class I have mentioned, taken before the clerk. The practice at the present time in that particular is exactly the same as it has been for some years past.
My right hon. friend referred to some action taken in 1888; at that time I believe the reference was to clerks whose position was that of permanent translators. They were permanent employees, as are the translators serving at the present time. If, on the part of His Honour the Speaker, there had been a dismissal of any persons belonging to the permanent organization, I think it would have been His Honour's duty to meet the obligation placed upon him by the statute. But clearly it could never have been the intention of the statute that the Speaker should report to the governor in council the suspension of every charman or charwoman, or the circumstances with respect to every page boy against whom complaint might be laid, or with respect to other employees performing temporary duties during the period of a session. I make that clear because I believe His Honour the Speaker has been most desirous of meeting every obligation placed upon him by statute, and has been anxious in no way to impinge upon the privileges of the house.
I now come to the question as to what is best to do. I thought my right hon. friend, when speaking a few days ago, was quite frank in stating that he would not for a moment be hypocritical enough to say that when there was a change of government all temporary employees should be retained by the incoming administration. He knew very well that almost immediately after he took office in 1930 there began to be a change in the personnel of the temporary employees of the House of Commons. I must say that I think it was perfectly reasonable that up to a certain point such a change should have been made. A Liberal government had been in office for several years. As a result a large number of pages, messengers, stenographers and all-year-round char people had been employed under the previous administration. In 1930 my right hon. friend had a large following in the House of Commons, and I must say that, having regard to the personal relationships of this class of employee with hon. members, he was quite right in feeling that there must be some recognition taken of the change of the per-
Dismissals-Mr. Mackenzie King

sonnel in the House of Commons, and that stenographers, messengers, pages and the like should be selected with some regard to political representation in the house itself. However, what was in his mind in that particular, I cannot say. It is true, certainly, that so far as the present administration is concerned, we would take the view, speaking generally, that an effort should be made to have the political complexion of temporary employees correspond in a general way with the political complexion of the House of Commons itself. I think my right hon. friend and members of his party should have a right to feel an absolute confidence in the persons they may have working with them as stenographers, for example, and that hon. members in other parts of the house and belonging to other groups should have equal confidence in those who are performing sessional services for them. Certainly members of the administration and their following should have that confidence. I do not think any hon. member would feel that the privileges of the house were in any way being infringed if observance along those lines were taken in the employment of temporary clerks and others for sessional purposes. Indeed, if that were not done, I can see where there might be considerable embarrassment to members generally.
My right hon. friend has inquired as to the best course	to pursue. This is a
difficult stage of the session at which finally to determine some of these matters. If the committees of the house were constituted, I would suggest that, immediately, there be a reference to the committee on privileges with respect to what is or should be the proper procedure to follow regarding the retention and dismissal of employees of the House of Commons when a change of government has taken place. The reference could be extended, if desired, to include the practice followed in past years. The inquiry could serve to furnish guidance not only to the administration holding office but also to administrations which may follow in subsequent years. The committees of the house, however, have not yet been constituted.
There is this further embarrassing feature, that as yet the house has not appointed a deputy speaker. As a result, His Honour the Speaker is in the embarrassing position of having to preside over a discussion which may take place between my right hon. friend and myself or between hon. members on this side of the house and hon. members opposite relating to his own action in this matter. I should think it most unfortunate if His Honour were obliged to preside over a debate or discussion of the kind. If a deputy speaker

had been appointed, I would suggest that the deputy speaker take the chair and permit debate of any length necessary.
Having given the matter some thought, I would suggest to my right hon. friend and hon. members-and I hope they will concur, that, when the house is properly organized, the different committees constituted, and the deputy speaker appointed, a motion might be made to refer to the committee on privileges the question as to the right and proper procedure to be adopted with respect to the retention or dismissal of employees of the House of Commons. I would expect that on that committee hon. members from all parts of the house would have representation. A report from the committee might then be made to the house, at which time we might have such discussion as may be necessary thereon. In considering the matter I think it would be proper for the committee to consider fully what was done after the change of government in 1930 and also all that has been done since the change of government last year. I believe that would be the most effective way of dealing with the matter, and one which would best serve to preserve the privileges of the house.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. BENNETT DISMISSAL OF CERTAIN HOUSE OF COMMONS EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
I must entirely disagree
with the construction placed :by the right hon. gentleman on sections 21 and 22 of chapter 145 of our statutes. If he had been trained perhaps in the practice of the law as he has been in the theory, he would have observed that section 22 does not apply to other than officers, clerks and messengers of the house. They must take the oath of allegiance. Section 21, to which I have referred, refers to the following persons: Clerk, officer, messenger or other person attendant on the House of Commons. The distinction is so clear that it is not necessary to do more than direct attention to it to see what the obvious inference is.
But further, the right hon. gentleman has failed to observe that it is with respect to those officials appointed by the crown that the report is made to the governor general. Page boys, the char service, persons appointed for the session, stenographers-all these some within the powers specially granted by the statute to the Speaker himself, it being provided that if they are appointed by the crown the Speaker may himself suspend or remove them if they ar.e guilty of misconduct, and if appointed by him he may suspend or dismiss them after inquiry. No one in this house has suggested at any time, so far as I know, that what is called the sessional staff, stenographers, messengers or page boys, and

15i
Dismissals-Mr. Bennett
so forth, should not be employed by the government under such conditions as the government of the day may think desirable, exercising either a broad and generous attitude ot a narrow partisan attitude towards the matter, as may be thought desirable. I said the other day that I am not questioning that that has been done and will continue to be done, I suppose, long after we have vanished from the scene. But the point at the moment is that the statute makes provision as to how those who are permanent shall be dealt with. The word "permanent" has two meanings. In the civil service the word "permanent" means one who comes under the civil service establishment, and cannot be removed from office except for cause. The temporary staff is a staff that does not fall within that category. But those who were dismissed this morning and yesterday were, many of them, men who had been here for years and who, if they were not removed, would continue to be here during the Test of their lives. One of them came here I believe in November, 1930, and has been here ever since. Another has been here since 1931, and there are some in exactly the same position in the char service who were appointed by my right hon. friend.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. BENNETT DISMISSAL OF CERTAIN HOUSE OF COMMONS EMPLOYEES
speechtext: No.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. BENNETT DISMISSAL OF CERTAIN HOUSE OF COMMONS EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Oh yes, in exactly the
same position. That is, they were appointed by the government of the day, and they went on and are going on to-day, to-morrow and the next day. Those I refer to in the char service and messenger service, and doorkeepers, have been drawing I believe, some of them, S60 for two weeks' work, others lesser amounts, and some have been paid by the day a certain sum for six days' work in the week.
There is a clear distinction between the permanent staff of this house and those who come here for sessional duties. I agree with the right hon. gentleman that stenographers are in the latter class; they are sessional employees only. That is also true of the page boys and of many other employees of the house. But there is a year to year service to which the right hon. gentleman has referred in which the employees will go on from now until they cease by death or otherwise to carry on their duties, unless they are removed by the Speaker. The only point I am making is that they have a right to know why they are removed. The statute says so. The distinction is made clear between the two classes.
I do agree with the right hon. gentleman that it is not perhaps in the interests of the position that parliament should occupy that
we should discuss the action of the Speaker at this moment, because we have not the papers before us. In 1888, however, the Speaker did table the papers, and I suggest that the papers should be tabled to-morrow. The right hon. gentleman is in error in assuming that the matter could not be dealt with before the committees are appointed because as a matter of fact, that is exactly what happened in 1888. When Sir Wilfrid Laurier brought the matter to the attention of the house the standing committees had not been appointed; in fact, the day before, Sir John Macdonald had made his motion that a select committee be named for the purpose of striking the standing committees. So the house was in exactly the position then as it is now; the committees had not been set up.
But I think what the right hon. gentleman has said about the method of dealing with the matter is not unsound, and if the Speaker will table the papers, which means that he will table, (a) the notices of dismissal that he had sent out by the sergeant-at-arms before the Speaker assumed office, and, (b) the notices that were sent out yesterday as to the dismissal of those who have been dismissed, with their names and the positions they occupied, I think that every end will be served. There are two things to keep in mind: first, that no injustice be done to people who have been serving this country in the various capacities I have named, and, secondly, that the privileges of parliament as provided by statute must not be, shall I say violated.
If the Speaker will file the papers as the Speaker did in 1888, I think the suggestion of the right hon. gentleman that in due season we can name a committee to deal with the matter will be entirely satisfactory; for then we shall have before us, not information which may or may not be entirely accurate- and as I said at the outset I am not undertaking to guarantee that the information I have received is accurate, although I believe it to be accurate, that men have been dismissed; but we shall have the facts before us.
The right hon. gentleman says that certain people have not taken the oath of allegiance. I think it would be very strange if they had, because the statute names only three classes, the clerk, the messengers and the other class I named.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. BENNETT DISMISSAL OF CERTAIN HOUSE OF COMMONS EMPLOYEES
speechtext: Officers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. BENNETT DISMISSAL OF CERTAIN HOUSE OF COMMONS EMPLOYEES
speechtext: And messengers.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. BENNETT DISMISSAL OF CERTAIN HOUSE OF COMMONS EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Yes, messengers, as I mentioned. But section 21 dealing with dis-

Dismissals-Mr. Mackenzie King
missals covers all those who are attendant on the House of Commons, meaning, I take it, all those who go on from year to year. The test would be this: How many of those men dismissed to-day or yesterday would have remained on had it not been for a change of administration? Were any of them guilty of misconduct? Were they proper persons to discharge the duties which they were fulfilling? -one a doorkeeper, another a charman, and so on. If the answers to these questions are satisfactorily given I think the matter can be readily disposed of. I do not think the position taken by the right hon. gentleman is an unfair one, and if as I say the Speaker will follow the practice that was followed by the Speaker in 1888-he was a Conservative Speaker-Sir Wilfrid Laurier was not at that time a Conservative, however much he may have been in his later days-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. BENNETT DISMISSAL OF CERTAIN HOUSE OF COMMONS EMPLOYEES
speechtext: He was never a Tory.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. BENNETT DISMISSAL OF CERTAIN HOUSE OF COMMONS EMPLOYEES
speechtext: Then later we can deal with the matter in the light of the documents we shall have before us, and know what charges, if any, have been made against the persons who have been dismissed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. BENNETT DISMISSAL OF CERTAIN HOUSE OF COMMONS EMPLOYEES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have no desire to add anything further to the discussion, nor for that matter to shut it off in any way. I hope hon. members will feel free to express their minds on this question, but I would like to point out to the house that, if the house will follow the course that I suggest, we may avoid the kind of difficulty that I see we are getting into. My right hon. friend was out of order when he spoke the second time, and I am out of order now.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. BENNETT DISMISSAL OF CERTAIN HOUSE OF COMMONS EMPLOYEES
speechtext: No, no, not on a question of privilege.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. BENNETT DISMISSAL OF CERTAIN HOUSE OF COMMONS EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
I am out of order now. It is impossible to have the question settled except by reference to His Honour the Speaker. If His Honour were appealed to in regard to my right hon. friend being out of order, my right hon. friend1 might not view the ruling in the same light as other hon. members of the house. I do think that what I have suggested is the best way of dealing with this matter. It is the fair, the open and aboveboard method to pursue, not only as a guide to the house during this parliament but the best way to be of service as well to subsequent parliaments.
As to the laying of any papers on the table,
I feel that a motion is required for that purpose which would give hon. members the 
opportunity of amending what is proposed by adding to, or subtracting from the motion or accepting it as presented. All papers that are necessary and all information that is desired can be placed before the committee on privileges under the reference that will be made. If the reference is not broad enough when it is submitted by the administration, and if it appeals to the house as being desirable to make it any broader, I give every assurance that the desires of the house will be acceded to.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. BENNETT DISMISSAL OF CERTAIN HOUSE OF COMMONS EMPLOYEES
speechtext: It will be necessary for me to move for papers.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. BENNETT DISMISSAL OF CERTAIN HOUSE OF COMMONS EMPLOYEES
speechtext: My right hon. friend may move for papers, but-

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. BENNETT DISMISSAL OF CERTAIN HOUSE OF COMMONS EMPLOYEES
speechtext: Quite the opposite course was taken under Sir Wilfrid.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. BENNETT DISMISSAL OF CERTAIN HOUSE OF COMMONS EMPLOYEES
speechtext: We will have to add to his motion the request that all papers, including papers covering dismissals made at the time my right hon. friend was in office, shall be brought down and tabled at the same time.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. BENNETT DISMISSAL OF CERTAIN HOUSE OF COMMONS EMPLOYEES
speechtext: Sir Wilfrid said that that was entirely beside the question.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: My right hon. friend need not think that anything that affects his administration is going to be beside this question, because what has been done up to the present does not begin to touch what my right hon. friend did in this regard when he was in office. On the orders of the day:

Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a question to the head of the government, an old cricketer and sportsman. This relates to a series of articles which have appeared in the papers. There has been some very bad advertising of Canada at the Olympic games by a Mr. Gilroy who says he is a representative of the government of Canada and will withdraw his team if he does not get his way there. I should like to quote shortly from the head-

The Address-Mr. Maclnnis
lines in this morning's Ottawa Journal, as follows:
Canada Ready Quit Olympic Hockey Games
Claim Playoff System Will Put Team at Disadvantage
New Bombshell Hits Tournament
Maple Leaf Squad Will Withdraw Unless Rule is Rescinded
Some weeks ago this gentleman referred to the sportsmen of England in a manner far from complimentary saying that this sport in England was a "racket." His late majesty was the greatest sportsman in the world and this row comes at a bad time and shows poor judgment in a time of mourning. This government has appropriated $10,000 for these games and if they are to cause bad relations internationally, if they are to be bad advertising for Canada, I think something should be done. I ask the head of the government to have an investigation made of this matter. There are rows before they leave, rows when they get over there and there -will [be probably rows when they come back, after these games are over.
I ask the hon. member to come to the point and put his question.

There was no need of your interruption, Mr. Speaker. I had to lay a foundation for the question. I think something should be done to stop this bad advertising. With the unsettled state of Europe these Olympic games as conducted create bad international feeling. The reference of Mr. Gilroy about British sport w'as in bad taste at a. time of mourning for his late majesty, and bad advertising for Canada. These votes should be confined to British empire games.

Mr. Speaker, I shall have to look up Hansard before I can give my hon. friend an accurate answer. As I understand him, he is taking exception to someone at the Olympic games claiming to be: a representative of Canada. People all over the world are only too ready to be that, and many are fond of expressing themselves in those terms. May I say to my hon. friend that if the one he has referred to is a representative of the government, he must have been so appointed by the previous administration. I think it is very doubtful that anyone participating in the Olympic games is a representative of the government of this country. Whether it is wise to vote money for the purpose of these games, or how such money should be voted, are matters that will come up for consideration should a like estimate be again before us. Such money as has been appropriated for the purpose mentioned by my
hon. friend was appropriated before the present administration came into office and was recommended by the government of which he was a supporter.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has pacified Europe; he ought to be able to pacify the Canadian Amateur Hockey Association.

Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned yesterday evening at six o'clock I was referring to some of the tactics employed by the Liberal party in British Columbia during the election campaign. I had not intended to bring this matter to the attention of the house until I heard the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) complain about what had been done in. Quebec. I then came to the conclusion that if it was a bad thing for Conservatives to appeal to racial and religious prejudices in the province of Quebec, it was an equally bad thing for Liberals to do the same thing in the province of British Columbia, and consequently it ought to be brought to the attention of the house. In that connection I was quoting from an article by Professor H. F. Angus of the university of British Columbia which appeared in the Canadian Forum. I shall not dwell on that subject much longer, but I should like to make one short quotation from this article. Professor Angus in this article stated two suppositions upon which it was possible to ex-
The Address

Mr. Maclnrds

plain this appeal to race prejudice, and he then stated:
If this is the explanation of the novel trend of liberalism, it is possible to argue that it was justified by results from the standpoint of the party. For Mr. King's right bower-
He was referring to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie)-
-was elected by a majority narrow enough to be interpreted as consisting of people who have morbid sensibilities where orientals are concerned. And yet, with all respect for the winning card, one may grudge the price that was paid.
I agree with that statement. If we cannot win elections, if we cannot make our voices heard in this country without appealing to racial and religious prejudices, then the price is too great as far as I am concerned.
I wish to make a few references to the speech from the throne. It does not contain a great deal that one can deal with definitely at this time, and I would say that if that large section of the electorate that voted for the Liberal candidates at the last election can find in the speech from the throne any justification for their vote, then they are not asking for very much.
The speech tells us something which of course we knew already-that unemployment continues to be Canada's most urgent problem. We all agree with that; but it gives no indication whatever of any immediate, or for that matter prospective, solution of that problem. Referring to the unemployment relief camps, I am glad that the government is taking steps to transfer them from the Department of National Defence to the Department of Labour. I do not know that it will make any great difference, though it may do away with any suggestion of the militarization of the camps. What the men in the camps are complaining about is not so much that the camps are under this or that department, as that they are compelled to stay in these camps without any hope far the future; and merely transferring the camps to the Department of Labour will not obviate that objection.
I was wondering why the government did not put the unemployment relief camps under the Minister of Finance rather than under the Minister of Labour. The Minister of Labour is a university man, and as far as I know he has had no experience in dealing with the unemployed. I understand, however, that the Minister of Finance has been in charge of a camp for unemployed at Lucerne, Quebec, for the last five years, and because of that he would possibly be the person best fitted to take care of unemployment. There might be

this difficulty, however, that if those with whom he would be dealing under the new conditions received the same consideration from society as those with whom he has come in contact during the last five years, they would not be satisfied to go back to the old conditions under which they have lived during these years.
The other morning in my mail I received two communications, and it was these that suggested to me the fitness of the Minister of Finance to look after the unemployed. The first communication was a letter from an old gentleman in the interior of Brtitish Columbia. His shaky handwriting was an indication of his age. He was complaining of having to live on $9 a month, which he was receiving in relief, and he referred to the items of diet on which he had to subsist-flour, rice, bacon and beans, a few prunes and tea and coffee. In the same mail I received the magazine of the Seigniory Club, a beautifully got up little publication, the best quality paper, a fine design on the cover, photographic illustrations of the very best; and I read in that magazine the qualifications for membership in the club. "Subject to social and racial restrictions"-this will appeal to my friends from British Columbia-membership in the club can be had, and it carries with it the privilege of hunting and fishing; whereas membership in other clubs that I have been referring to, the unemployment camps, carries with it the privilege of working for twenty cents a day. There is some difference. Life membership in the Seigniory Club costs only $2,000, the ordinary membership being $250 for initiation and $125 annually.
I looked up the relief allowance in Vancouver and this is what I found. If you take the total in relief allowed for a man and wife for one year, for food, clothing and shelter, at the end of the year they will have received $1 short of the amount necessary to buy a year's membership in the Seigniory club. A little further on in the same magazine I have mentioned I read the following:
Nature in the raw this winter in the Seigniory Club forest will be a little less raw than usual, thanks to the distribution of several hundred pounds of bean and molasses cakes. The younv deer get their proper number of vitamins from these, and then when normal feed has grown scarce and the snow is so deep they cannot labour through it, the guides and rangers cut brush and lay it on the trail so they can get it without difficulty.
The man who wrote to me about the difficulty of carrying on on $9 a month pointed out that he was not allowed any sugar. There was no thought taken of vitamins as far as he

was concerned, and there is very little thought taken for the 1,200,000 people who are on relief in Canada at the present time-no thought as to whether or not they have the proper amount of vitamins. It is much better to be a deer in the forest of the Seigniory Club than a Canadian on relief in this country, because the one receives some consideration while the other gets very little.
I do not think I can be accused of wrongly interpreting the policy of the government when I say that its hope of bringing about an improvement in Canadian conditions is based largely on the extension of our foreign trade. The following reference in the speech from the throne leads me to that conclusion:
Every effort will be made to close the camps altogether at as early a date as expanding employment opportunities permit.
It seems to me that if the men in the relief camps are to remain there until expanding production is brought about by an extension of foreign trade, their hope of getting away from the camps in the near future, or indeed in the distant future, is very remote.
Having touched on the question of trade, I will now take such little time as is left to me to deal further with that question, a question about which I believe there is a great deal of confusion at the present time. I am going to make a statement that to many members of this house may seem strange. I am not only going to make that statement; I also think I can prove it. The statement is this: Under our present capitalist system an extension of trade, or increased trade, will ultimately lead to a reduction in trade. That may seem a contradiction, but capitalism is full of contradictions, and, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) the other day, these contradictions are becoming very apparent at the present time.
If we look over the history of the past hundred years, the development of trade and commerce, we find that there is hardly a nation on earth that has not increased its trade during that time. Indeed the last hundred years has been an era of universal trade expansion, and it goes without saying that this trade expansion has been universally beneficial. The question may be asked as to why this trade expansion cannot continue indefinitely. We might as well ask why a man cannot continue to grow in stature after he has reached maturity. Trade cannot continue to increase because through the extension of trade every country has become provided with the means that will make it more and more self sufficient. Whether or not there is a definite purpose there is a definite 12739-11
The Address-Mr. Maclnnis
result which follows the trade expansion of the last hundred years; as I said a moment ago the effect of that has been to make the nations of the world more and more self sufficient in the matter of production. Following that I may say that what we are pleased to term "economic nationalism" is just as natural in the development of the nations of the world to-day as stiff joints are in old men. It is merely an effort on the part of the nations of the world, in an era of declining trade, to protect themselves, and whether we like it or not it will go on until we change our system of production and distribution.
Now let me give you an example of the development of trade, trade as we know it to-day, trade under the capitalist system, and when we refer to the capitalist system we have in mind that period beginning with the use of motive power to drive machinery. That form of production was first used in Great Britain towards the end of the eighteenth century, and I think it is correct to say that the textile industry was the first industry to be highly developed under the new method. That industry in Great Britain increased immensely from 1776 to 1913. We find that in the latter year the exports of British cotton reached the very large total of 7,075,000,000 yards. Sixteen years later, however, in 1929, British exports of cotton goods shrank to 3,765,000,000 yards, a decrease of 47 per cent. Coming down a little later, to 1933, we find the decrease still going on, with the exports of that year not up to the three billion yard mark.
What is the reason for this shrinkage in British exports of cotton goods? There is only one answer; it is that Great Britain not only exported cotton goods during that period; she also exported the machinery used to manufacture cotton goods, and that machinery was sent to those countries which formerly bought British cotton goods. As a result these countries are now able to manufacture their own cotton goods to supply their own markets. More than that, they are now competitors with Great Britain for a share of the foreign market still available, and this foreign market will continue to diminish-

Mr. Speaker, it has been suggested by the social credit party, meeting in caucus, that I make the following statement, which correctly expresses the position we take with regard to the speech from the throne:
We believe the time for cooperation has come, and we are supporting the motion because the speech from the throne indicates many great reforms, although it does not contain, in our estimation, an adequate and permanent solution to our economic ills.
I have a few things in mind which I feel should be said at this time. I conceive parliament to be a committee of citizens appointed and paid by the people to transact public business and promote and safeguard the welfare of the people of this country. If parliament continues to do that it merits the support of the electorate. When it ceases to do that it should be removed from office with the same unconcern as that with which a farmer would scrap a rusty plough that had ceased to serve.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the supreme task confronting this parliament and this country at the present time is the winning of industrial democracy. As a member of the Anglo-Saxon race I am glad that after a thousand years of struggle for political democracy we are in a far happier position than some of the other nations of the world. Rut political democracy, unless it is accompanied by industrial democracy-which means the right of all the people to share in the abundance of the earth-is a mere shell, formless and meaningless.
I want to refer to the passing of His Majesty King George V; I want to refer to the man and his identification of himself with human problems. My leader, the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) quoted the other day these words from his late majesty's address on the occasion of the imperial economic conference in London in 1932:
It cannot be beyond the power of man so to use the vast resources of the *world as to ensure the material progress of civilization.
You will notice that he did not say, to ensure the progress of the Bank of England, or the Bank of Montreal; he said "civilization."
No diminution in these resources has taken place. On the contrary, discovery, invention and organization have multiplied their possibilities to such an extent that abundance of production has itself created new problems.

Now, Mr. Speaker, what manner of man is this who, while a king, can yet espouse the cause of the common people throughout the world? I thought during the days of official mourning here the king would expect something more than black draperies and expressions of sorrow; he would expect the people of his empire to remember his words and to act upon them. And it may be-who can tell-that somewhere within the shoreless vast of this universe he may be looking down upon us now from the luminous slopes of the stars, saying to us, in the words that the psalmist might have used, How long, 0 Lord, will men continue to pay lip homage and forget humanity; humanity and its struggle forward to a higher plane, a state of peace?
I wish to say a word or two about the situation confronting this parliament, indeed confronting all the peoples of the world. George Bernard Shaw in one of his recent plays says that the other planets use this world for a lunatic asylum. Thousands of years ago our ancestors, who lived precariously on the thin edge of starvation, often died because there was not enought to eat. If we could by some process of reincarnation bring back to this vale of tears some of those luckless progenitors of ours and let them see the spectacle of millions of men and women cold, hungry and miserable in the presence of huge piles of food and clothing, what conclusion could they reach other than that we are all crazy? The difference, I suppose he would say, is this, that in the ordinary lunatic asylum the inmates only are supposed to be crazy, but in this one the keepers as well are crazy.
I think there is a general recognition of the fact that the remedies proposed at the present time are not only unworkable, but, to use the words of the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, leader of the Conservative party in the Senate, are archaic palliatives. I will quote Mr. Meighen's own words:
But the naked and unassailable truth, which only stupidity can prevent anyone from seeing, is that if the United States were to be brought back to-morrow to the peak production of 1929, a production which the world utterly failed to consume or to purchase, there would remain in that country no fewer than six and probably eight millions of unemployed, representing virtually one-third of its whole earning population. What is true there is true in other lands, hut the enigma is greater and perhaps the lesson ought to be clearer when one looks upon the situation as a phenomenon of the United States. That is essentially an immensely wealthy country, the greatest self contained country in the world. If it were a planet it would not need to trade with any other planet in order to multiply the wealth of man. It produces either all that mankind

The Address-Mr. Rowe (Athabaska)
needs or effective substitutes therefor, and if it could devise a plan for putting to work those millions who are now unemployed it would be a happy land. When we see that country struggling in the throes of one of the most terrible depressions that any nation has ever had to face, when we see its people in such desperate straits that even the people of old England are prosperous in comparison, we are forced to think that something further is needed than mere amendments to tariffs and the holding of international conferences, or the trying of other and somewhat archaic medicines that have been applied to the body politic in the past.
I believe, sir, it is an easily demonstrable fact that the Dominion of Canada, perhaps the most richly endowed with vital natural resources of any Land on, earth, is not only capable of supporting its present population of eleven millions, and giving to them everything in the shape of food, clothing, shelter and cultural opportunities, but could support a population of probably five times that number. That statement I think cannot be challenged. Yet what do we find? We have unemployment, we have the dole, that humiliating and degrading thing, a blot on civilization. Here I should like to quote the words of our present king. When Prince of Wales, visiting the coal mines in Wales, he used these words; they were quoted by my leader the other day, but they will bear repetition:
What a ghastly mess it all is! It makes me positively sick. What is the cause of all this? It cannot go on, it is a blot on England.
Those are the words of His Majesty the King of England. I can only say again that there is a general recognition of the fact that these contradictions are inherent in the system, as the speaker iwho preceded me said, and it is the work of this parliament to give constructive leadership in the solution of these and related problems.
I should like to refer to something that lion, members in this chamber, surrounded by comfort, everything that exalts and embellishes our civilized life, sitting in this comfortable room with messengers and servants, warmth and brightness, might be tempted to forget. There is a statement which I feel it my duty to make. I say more in sorrow than in anger that while the debate was proceeding yesterday, while the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) was describing some of the awful and pathetic conditions which prevailed among the poor people of the west, victims of this failure by the leaders of men to solve 'our problems, some hon. members in the chamber seemed to think that those conditions were a joke. I wonder if they have not forgotten the people 12739-lli
who pay, or try to pay the taxes, who pay for the building and protection we enjoy, who have made every sacrifice, who have contributed to this country and its development and are now being left destitute.
I have thought it wise to place on Hansard some observations of the Hon. Senator Pascal Poirier, now deceased, but whom some hon. members in this chamber may have known. He said:
As a result of these conferences our economic situation will very likely be improved. Improved, but not healed. The dreaded cancer will remain. Something must be found which will extirpate it, and this with no long delay, for the cancer grows alarmingly.
The murmur that reaches parliament from the streets is now subdued, for things have not come to a crisis, and the dole appeases the hunger of the multitude. But when the public treasury is exhausted and the dole is no longer forthcoming that murmur will change into a malediction. Hearken to the suppressed rumble! It comes from gatherings of unemployed from Victoria to Sydney, from prisons like Portsmouth, St. Vincent de Paul, Dorchester, from everywhere. And what will happen, what can happen, if the rabble, so-called, run amuck and break all restraints?
Remember what happened in France during the revolution of 1793. Look at what happened in Portugal not so long ago. Look at what is happening to-day in Russia, in Spain, in Mexico. The Czar of all the Russias, the grandees of Spain and Portugal, the clergy of Mexico, once all-powerful, were scattered like dry leaves in a hurricane when the people rose in anger.
All that may be true, but are we, the governing class in democratic Canada, not in a position to quell insurrections? No, my friends, we are not, if lines are drawn and sides taken. Since the granting of manhood and womanhood suffrage, the majority governs, as it did before, but the axis of majority has shifted. There is even no necessity of a revolution in Canada to put the administration down and out. It can be done constitutionally, at the polls. Let all the malcontents unite, it is possible that later on they may secure a majority at the polls. What will happen then? They will climb up and we shall climb down, we senators as well as others. If, to use a vulgar expression, we kick, they will look upon us as disturbers of public peace, as insurgents, as undesirables; and, if they deem it necessary for the preservation of order and good government, they may confiscate our properties and show us the road to exile. Such things have happened elsewhere and are actually happening.
Nothing like this is likely to occur in Canada, because our labouring classes have so far had no grievous charge to lay against their employers; they were never oppressed or wronged by them, and they, as much as we, favour the continuation of the present political regime. But let discontent grow, let the number of unemployed increase to dangerous proportions, let a crisis come, and no one can tell what may happen.
Those are not the words of an agitator, but those of a former member of the Senate of Canada.
164	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Rowe (Athabaska)
I have one or two observations to make concerning the international situation of the League of Nations. As was stated a few days ago by the hon. member for Weybum, the League of Nations is an organization of about fifty nations banded together to create among nations a state of law and order where formerly international anarchy had prevailed. As I see it, the league was designed to do for nations what criminal and civil courts were designed to do for individuals. For instance, several hundred years ago the institution of duelling was outlawed, and through the establishment of courts disputes arising betwen individuals were taken before an impartial tribunal and there, in the calm light of judicial detachment, were adjudicated upon. Passions were quelled; a judge would rule one man right and the other wrong, or partly so. But the institution of duelling which because it resulted in brutal killings and great injustice had been outlawed by the conscience of mankind was not a success for many years. We have record of many duels being fought after the practice was legally outlawed. Many thousands of years ago, before the dawn of civilization, tribes resorted to mass murder in order to settle disputes arising among them. The conscience of mankind crystallized in the League of Nations, a tribunal set up to restore order out of anarchy and to afford an opportunity to hear the voices of the smaller nations.
We cannot expect the League of Nations to be anything but a reflection of the institutions of nations composing it; it would not be reasonable to expect more. Therefore, while predatory individuals abused the courts we now find nations abusing the League of Nations to further selfish interests which certain small groups within those nations are trying to serve. The hon. member for Wey-burn (Mr. Douglas) made some observations about the Anglo-Persian Oil Company furnishing oil to Italian troops. While we endorse the idea of the League of Nations and believe it is the only hope of mankind for preventing war in the future, we deprer cate the tendency on the part of certain nations to allow predatory or unscrupulous groups of interests within those nations to use the league for any such purposes, and our policy would be to strengthen the league by every possible means and to insist upon an impartial imposition of economic sanctions. I w'ould like to commend the government for the stand it took in what conceivably was a very dangerous situation, which might have resulted, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said the other day, in a European conflagration which 
would have involved us all. We want to remember that the situation in Europe is largely the result of our own failures in the past, of our failures and the failures of diplomacy in general.
I think it could not be challenged with regard to war that the spectre of all the great wars in history will rise up in the day of judgment and point an accusing finger at the leaders of men, because it has been through their stupidity and ineptitude that the common people have been led to the shambles. The failure to recognize the equal worth of other peoples and nations, the failure to recognize the inalienable right of every nation to access to raw materials with which to build a civilization commensurate with our own, is one of the efficient causes of war. The balance of power is a political cause of war, because once any nation, actuated by whatever motives of self defence, assumes a position of superiority or desires to dominate, it is immediately challenged by every other nation and then we have an armament race. What is at the back of it? Simply this:	We have here a country that is
able to support fifty million people. It is not supporting eleven million people, and yet we are shipping out of this country our vital natural resources in the form of finished goods in a mad scramble for markets that do not exist. Then collisions occur between the nations, and then sometimes we are asked to go out and shed our blood. The system itself is the cause of this.
President Wilson said in St. Louis just before he died, and I do not think anyone here who has studied economics and the economic causes of war would disagree:
Is there a man or woman, is there a child in this audience, who does not know that the seeds of war are sown in hot, successful commercial rivalry?
Then it has been found necesary to plunge the world into war as a result of the failure of the system, and the common people are led to the shambles because the leaders of men have not been able to formulate an intelligent policy for producing and distributing the wealth of the world.
What will our policy be? I would like to suggest one or two things, and may I say that I am here with an open mind, anxious to cooperate and to offer some suggestions to the government. As I came through Calgary on my way down here I picked up a copy of the Calgary Herald and read a report of an address to the Canadian Club given by Doctor Kerby, principal of the Mount Royal College, Calgary and I think this will be of interest to the right hon.

The Address-Mr. Rowe (Athabaska)
leader of the opposition because I noticed that he introduced the speaker. This is what Doctor Kerby says about our foreign policy:
Canada will come into a foremost place among the nations of the world not because of her unparalleled scenic beauty, her vast extent of territory, or her inexhaustible natural resources, but by virtue of the thought-power of her people and their leaders.
The hope of Canada lies in the quality of its life, the ability of the people to assimilate new ideals and standards, and to incorporate them into our national life.
It lies also in a national ideal-not founded upon wealth, or military power, but upon a broad concept of human helpfulness and human service, based on humanity and Christianity. There is no security for the nation, outside of goodwill; there is no impregnable fortress except brotherhood, no invincible armament except service and no prevailing diplomacy except the truth.
I submit that that is a sound basis for our foreign policy. I want to quote also from Victor Hugo's presidential address at the peace conference in 1849. He said:
A day will come when you, France-you, Russia-you, Italy-you, England-you, Germany-all of you nations of the continent- shall, without losing your distinctive qualities and your glorious individuality, blend in a higher unity and form a European fraternity, even as Normandy. Brittany, Burgundy, Lorraine, Alsace, all the French provinces, have become blended.
A day will come when war shall seem as absurd and impossible between Paris and London, betwen St. Petersburg and Berlin, as between Rouen and Amiens, between Boston and Philadelphia. A day will come when bullets and bombs shall be replaced by ballots by the universal suffrage of the people, by the sacred arbitrament of a great sovereign senate, which shall be to Europe what the parliament is to England, what the diet is to Germany, what the legislative assembly is to France.
A day will come when a cannon ball shall be exhibited in our museums as an instrument of torture is now, and men shall marvel that such things could be. A day will come when shall be seen those two immense groups, the United States of America and the United States of Europe, in face of each other, extending hand to hand over the ocean, exchanging their products, their commerce, their industry, their arts, their genius-clearing the earth, colonizing deserts, and ameliorating creation, under the eye of the Creator.
Well, the twentieth century is here, and I wonder if we in this parliament by the policies we initiate shall see the fulfilment of that prophecy uttered one hundred years ago. If it is true, and I believe it is true and is accepted by the leaders of this government and by everyone who thinks seriously about a solution of this problem, that the methods that are now proposed cannot solve it, why do we not change those methods? Why do we not dispassionately and detachedly study
this problem? Why adopt the procrustean method of reasoning, chopping off the feet of theories that do not fit the facts and stretching out theories that do not fit the facts? Why not adopt the method of inductive reasoning, analysing the facts before us as a scientist would and reaching a conclusion after an examination of the facts? We try to find an open mind on this question, a mind that has striven conscientiously to rid itself of prepossessions and prejudices and to understand the elements of good in every one of these conflicting economic and political philosophies before commencing destructive criticism. At least a man should learn from experience. We have not got that mind. Perhaps I should put on Hansard a little poem which may throw some light on the reason why we change so slowly. It reads:
Said Life Force to Amoeba,
As she wiggled in the tide:
"It's time you're evoluting,
So get busy and divide."
But Amoeba, from Tradition,
Argued it is plain to view Where there's been one organism There can't suddenly be two!
But there were.
Said Changed Environment to Amphibian,

We often hear the slogan: In time of peace prepare for war. I suggest that we change that slogan to read: In time of peace establish peace so firmly that it can never be success-

fully attacked again. I think of the founder of Christianity standing on the hill overlooking Jerusalem and uttering these words:	"O

I have only a minute or two left and I should like to place on Hansard an item which appeared in the Review of Reviews entitled Can Britannia Rule the Waves? I make reference to this article because of the Japanese. Yesterday in Ottawa we met a gentleman from China and he suggested that we should do something to revert the status of Manchukuo so that it would not longer be recognized as a nation among nations. We must remember that when Admiral Perry blasted open the harbour of Tokyo in 1852 he put into the hands of the Japanese the instruments of modem warfare. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to speak on the address, but considerable has been said about wheat, and after listening to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) I think it is right and proper that I should make a few observations.
First, I should like to congratulate the mover, (Mr. Slaght) and the seconder (Mr. 
Fournier, Maisonneuve) of the address upon the spendid manner in which they acquitted themselves in making their first speeches in this chamber. Many important questions mentioned in the speech from the throne have been discussed already and I shall not give any time to these matters, paying more attention to the question of wheat. An opportunity will be presented later to deal with these other matters when they come before the house in due course.
I should like to clear up one misunderstanding. The charge has been made on two occasions, first by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and then yesterday by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, that the Conservative party was responsible for interjecting the wheat question into the Assiniboia by-election. I think it is well known that the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) was either in California or on the sea at that time. 'He was not in Canada. As the only Conservative member from Saskatchewan, I can assure the house that I never discussed that by-election with him at all. I admit that Mr. Turnbull of Regina and myself took some little part in it, but the first appearance I made was on January 2. The records and reports of the speeches made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) will show that during the last week in December, and even at his nomination, he referred to the wheat question in addresses he made. At every address he made he referred to the wheat board and criticized Mr. McFarland and his operations. The wheat question was interjected into that campaign by the hon. gentleman himself.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a point of order-I should like to make this correction. I did not discuss the wheat question or, Mr. McFarland at my nomination convention.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The reports
show that the hon. member discussed it on many other occasions, and I shall probably refer to them later. The point I wish to make is that the wheat question was being discussed in that campaign long before I got there. I did not get there until January 2. I was in Winnipeg during Christmas week and arrived home on December 29. I found awaiting me there letters from all parts of Saskatchewan protesting against the action of the wheat committee of the cabinet in dismissing the advisory committee of the wheat board. I had telephone messages from different parts of Assiniboia; I heard from Manor, Ar.cola, Kipling and other places. I was told that as I was the only Conservative member from

The Address-Mr. Perley (Qu'Appelle)
Saskatchewan it was felt that it was my duty to go down and defend Mr. McFarland, and I went down. I say that neither the Conservative party nor my leader had anything to do with that action. While I was in Winnipeg I gathered some information with respect to what had taken place during the first week or ten days that the new board was in action, and I may have something to say about that later.
There were, of course, many other issues in that campaign, but I will not take time to discuss them. We heard yesterday from the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) the reasons for the dismissal of the McFarland board. Let me observe that anything I do say with respect to any member of the government is not spoken in a personal sense at all but purely from the point of view of criticism of their policy. I have the greatest respect for the Minister of Trade and Commerce and for other ministers to whom I may refer; I have the greatest respect for them as men, and I am merely criticizing their policy. I think that the country wishes us to criticize in a constructive way anything that calls for criticism, and certainly wheat is the most important problem in the west.
The minister stated that the committee believed that in Great Britain there was growing up a sales resistance. Possibly so; he quoted yesterday from editorials and newspaper clippings to that effect. But let us see what this new commission is; let us see who the persons are that constitute it and what has been their attitude. The new commission is composed of Mr. Murray, Mr. Mclvor and Mr. Shaw. As regards the first two mentioned gentlemen, there is no doubt in the world that they have had wide experience in the marketing of grain. I believe they are capable in every way, and if they would direct their attention to marketing in the interests of the farmers they could possibly do a very creditable job. The point I wish to make however is that these three men are on leave of absence from the respective organizations or institutions with which they were formerly employed. They are on leave of absence for ten months or a year. Dean Shaw of the university of Saskatchewan is on leave for ten months. Now this fact I say indicates the policy of the present government towards the wheat board. I wish to direct the attention of hon. members to something which possibly they' do not know and which I do not think the. public generally is aware of. Bearing in mind the fact I have just mentioned, let us think of the amendment that was proposed by Mr. Ralston on the night of the first of July
last, when we met in the railway committee room to put the finishing touches on the bill. The chairman having said, "This is the bill," Mr. Ralston proposed the following amendment which will be found in the records of the committee :
Mr. Ralston, seconded by Mir. Stewart, moved an amendment to the bill as section 10, namely:	^
The operations of the board shall not extend beyond the 15th day of August, 1936, except for the purpose of sale and realization of assets, collections, payments and generally for the winding up of the affairs and business of the board.
Compare that with the fact that these men are on leave of absence for ten months and, I submit, it is a fair indication of what the policy of the present government is towards the wheat board and that system of marketing.
Now what about the advisory committee? The farmers of western Canada are protesting very strongly against the dismissal of the advisory committee. The bill provided for a committee of seven, on which there were four representatives of the farmers.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Is it not a fact that a former member of the board, Mr. Grant, was also merely given leave of absence to act on the board?

speechtext:
Well, so far as the policy of the late government is concerned, there is no doubt about that policy with respect to the board and its sale of wheat in western Canada. The farmers now have no representatives; they have been replaced by a committee of the cabinet: the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler), the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), and the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Crerar). These are excellent gentlemen, and two of them have had wide experience in the grain business, the Minister of Finance and the Minister of the Interior; and the Minister of Agriculture has no doubt had considerable experience himself, having held a very important position in Saskatchewan.
I am not at all criticizing the intention of these gentlemen, but I will remind the house of a certain election that was held in Saskatchewan in 1934. It is well within the

The Address-Mr. Perley (Qu'Appelle)
memory of many hon. members what took place on June 19, 1934, in Saskatchewan, where there was an election that returned the Minister of Agriculture with a splendid majority. We have heard in this house something about pamphlets used in the last federal election. Well, I have here one that was used in that particular election and it speaks about dollar wheat:
Dollar wheat will give you a job and enable you to own your own home. Dollar wheat will pay for your light and water and give you a telephone. Dollar wheat will pay your grocery bill and buy boots, shoes and clothing for the whole family. Vote Liberal.
On the other side I find this:
Dollar wheat will provide a surplus for a "rainy day." Vote Liberal.
That pamphlet did its work. It was found in every cream can in Saskatchewan for weeks before the election, and in every motor car on Saturday nights in the towns. But there is not a single thing there to indicate how the promised result would be brought about.

speechtext:
This is what it says:
Trade will bring dollar wheat.
Great Britain is willing and anxious to trade.
Of course; the Ottawa agreements make it possible for us to trade.
European countries are anxious to trade. The Liberal party is anxious to trade.
I have here a statement by the Minister of Finance that our trade was lost, our markets in Europe were lost, as far as wheat was concerned.

speechtext: Read it now, the exact statement. .
